b.bio: This catalogue entry is a collective designation for various authors associated with the Latin Fathers tradition, holding conciliar documents including the acts of the councils and assemblies of Tribur, Quierzy, Attigny, and Koblenz.
b.s: This record represents multiple historical participants of Carolingian-era synods and assemblies rather than an identifiable individual.

w: Collection of the decrees of the Roman pontiffs

b.bio: Dionysius Exiguus (c. 470 – c. 544) — Dionysius Exiguus ('the Humble') was a monk born in Scythia Minor (modern Romania) who lived in Rome from around 500 until his death before 544. Cassiodorus calls him a Scythian, learned in both Greek and Latin; later writers honor him as an abbot, though Cassiodorus describes him as still an ordinary monk late in life. He translated 401 church canons from Greek into Latin — the Apostolic Canons, Nicaea, Constantinople, Chalcedon, Sardica — and compiled the decretals of popes from Siricius to Anastasius II. His Collectiones canonum Dionysianae carried great authority in the West. At Pope John I's request he prepared in 525 the Easter reckoning that introduced Anno Domini dating. The works here include his canonical collections and Easter letters alongside his Latin translations: Gregory of Nyssa on the creation of man, the Life of Pachomius, and the finding of John the Baptist's head. A Synodal Letter is also held under his name, though some works long attributed to him (e.g. Cyril of Alexandria's synodical letter) are now assigned to Marius Mercator.
b.s: The works held here are the foundations of Western canon law and the Easter computus that gave the Christian calendar its AD numbering.

b.bio: This entry represents a collective heading in the catalogue under the Latin Fathers associated with the transmission of the Code of Canons of the Universal Church.
b.s: Denotes the collective ecclesiastical bodies whose synodal decrees and canons formed the foundational jurisprudence of the early Church.

w: Code of Canons of the Universal Church

b.bio:
Various Councils (unknown) — This is a collective attribution, not a single author: the library files under this name the canons of an early church council as printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 67. The material preserved here is disciplinary and doctrinal legislation rather than the work of one writer. The canons regulate ordination and provincial church order, require bishops to be ordained by provincial bishops with metropolitan confirmation, mandate twice-yearly provincial synods to review excommunications, and provide that excommunication imposed by one province binds all provinces. They also legislate against named parties: the Eustathians most heavily, and briefly against Nestorius, the Novatianists, Celestius, and the Paulianists.

Dionysius Exiguus (c. 470 – c. 544) — Dionysius Exiguus ('the Humble') was a monk born in Scythia Minor (modern Romania) who lived in Rome from around 500 until his death before 544. Cassiodorus calls him a Scythian, learned in both Greek and Latin; later writers honor him as an abbot, though Cassiodorus describes him as still an ordinary monk late in life. He translated 401 church canons from Greek into Latin — the Apostolic Canons, Nicaea, Constantinople, Chalcedon, Sardica — and compiled the decretals of popes from Siricius to Anastasius II. His Collectiones canonum Dionysianae carried great authority in the West. At Pope John I's request he prepared in 525 the Easter reckoning that introduced Anno Domini dating. The works here include his canonical collections and Easter letters alongside his Latin translations: Gregory of Nyssa on the creation of man, the Life of Pachomius, and the finding of John the Baptist's head. A Synodal Letter is also held under his name, though some works long attributed to him (e.g. Cyril of Alexandria's synodical letter) are now assigned to Marius Mercator.
b.s: The work held here is a window into how the early church governed itself by conciliar canon: ordination, discipline of clergy, second marriages, and the binding force of synodal excommunication across provinces.

b.bio: Venantius Monaldinus is represented in the library by two pieces in PL 85: a preface and an epistle concerning the ancient Spanish liturgy. They argue that the Mozarabic rite differs from the Greek, Ambrosian, and Roman rites; that the Spanish churches kept one liturgy until Gregory VII; and that councils and Isidore attest it, citing Benedict XIV and Gregory VII against what is 'commonly handed down.' No surviving record gives dates or offices for Monaldinus himself.
b.s: His preface is a defense of the antiquity and distinctness of the Mozarabic liturgy, built from conciliar and Isidorean evidence (as recorded in the library's summary of the work).

b.bio: No surviving record concerns this author: all four describe Valentinus the second-century Egyptian Gnostic, founder of the Roman and Alexandrian gnostic schools, who died c. 160–161 — a different person of the same name, so they cannot be used. The only evidence for this author is the library record. It holds a single work under his name: a two-page Latin epistle printed in Migne's PL 44 (a volume of Augustinian material) treating grace, free will, justification, prayer, sin, the church, and last things, asserting that grace is given apart from merit through the redeemer and that free will exists but is healed by grace. It cites an Evodius ('lord father'), a presbyter Sabinus, a brother Florus, and 'the lord pope,' and answers dissenting brothers who boast of free will. These correspondents and themes place the author in the Latin anti-Pelagian circle, not among second-century Gnostics.
b.s: On the evidence of the library record alone, the work held here is a short Latin epistle arguing that free will, conscience, and progress in holiness depend wholly on unmerited grace, written against brothers who boasted of free will.

b.bio: The library holds a single item under the name Valerius: a dedicatory letter printed in Migne's Latin series alongside the sermons of Zeno of Verona (PL 11). None of The surviving records describe this person: they cover Valerius Maximus, the first-century Roman historian and moralist; Valerius of Saragossa, bishop and martyr who died c. 315 under Diocletian's persecution; and Valerius of El Bierzo, the seventh-century Visigothic ecclesiastical writer. Those are different men with different works, and their biographies cannot be transferred here. What can be said comes from the letter itself as recorded in the library: it addresses Pope Sixtus V, cites Bernard, and argues that Zeno's sermons merit accurate re-edition.
b.s: His work here is the dedicatory letter prefacing Zeno of Verona's sermons, asserting that unbroken episcopal succession preserves the true faith and that the norm of faith and life flows from the Roman see, where the pope is Peter in power and Christ in unction.

b.bio: The library's author is Verus Ruthenensis episcopus, a bishop whose two short letters are printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina vol. 80, dated to 625 by Documenta Catholica Omnia. He must not be confused with Verus I of Vienne, a fourth-century bishop who attended the Council of Arles in 314, nor with any modern 'Ruthenian' writer such as Meletius Smotrytsky: the Latin 'Ruthenensis' here refers to the Rutheni of Gaul, not to Rus'. The sources give no birthplace, death date, or career beyond the episcopal title.
b.s: His surviving letters in this library treat the Church and take issue with one Sulpitius, whom the text addresses as 'the lord Sulpitius'; they survive only as brief fragments, so he matters chiefly as an example of seventh-century Gallic episcopal correspondence.

b.bio: Victor of Capua is known only through his epitaph and his writings. He became bishop of Capua in February 541 and died in April 554 after an episcopate of thirteen years; the Roman Martyrology commemorates him on 17 October as distinguished for learning and holiness. His best-known work is the Codex Fuldensis, one of the oldest manuscripts of the Vulgate, which he directed, revised, and corrected; it replaces the four Gospels with a single harmony which he attributed, with some doubt, to Tatian. The library holds his Interpretation of Gospel Harmonies under his name in PL 68.
b.s: The works here are exegesis on the Gospel harmony: they argue that Christ's passion fulfilled the scriptures, that seeing Christ is seeing the Father, that the harmony is Tatian's rather than Ammonius's, and that ten canons exhaust the combinations of Gospel concord.

b.bio: Victor of Carthage was a bishop known from a letter addressed to Pope Theodore I around 646, in which he announced his elevation to the episcopal chair and accepted the doctrine of two wills in Christ. He should not be confused with Victor Vitensis (Victor of Vita), the fifth-century historian of the Vandal persecution; the works held here are epistles of the seventh-century bishop, not that history. The letters defend Chalcedonian Christology against Patriarch Paul of Constantinople and other innovators.
b.s: His surviving letters are evidence for how African bishops aligned with Rome against Monothelite innovation at Constantinople, affirming two wills and two operations in Christ.

b.bio: Victor II was born Gebhard of Calw (Dollnstein-Hirschberg), son of Count Hartwig of Calw and a kinsman of Emperor Henry III. Appointed Bishop of Eichstätt in 1042 at age twenty-four, he became the emperor's most influential councillor and was nominated by Henry as Leo IX's successor, consecrated pope on 13 April 1055. He continued reform through synods at Florence, Lyon, and Toulouse condemning clerical marriage and simony, and after Henry III's death in October 1056 served as guardian of the infant Henry IV. He died at Arezzo on 28 July 1057.
b.s: The letters held here are chiefly diplomas protecting monasteries: they confirm possessions under apostolic privilege, exempt monks from uninvited episcopal jurisdiction, secure free abbatial election, and anathematize violation of papal privilege — including against the archbishop of Cologne and imperial intrusion into church goods.

b.bio: Claudius Marius Victor (also printed Victorinus or Victorius) was a rhetor of Marseille, known to us through Gennadius of Massilia, who records his death under Theodosius II and Valentinian III, around 446. He wrote a hexameter poem on Genesis, the Aletheia, intended for the instruction of the young, and a verse letter to the abbot Salomon blaming the devastations of Sarmatians, Vandals, and Alans on human sin, especially sexual vice. Note that he must not be confused with the fourth-century African grammarian Marius Victorinus Afer treated elsewhere.
b.s: His works here retell Genesis from creation to Sodom in classical epic form, arguing creation ex nihilo against proponents of an eternal world and against pagan astrologers, diviners, idolaters, and oracles.

b.bio: Victricius, son of a Roman legionary, served as a soldier in Gaul before his conversion; he refused military service as a Christian and was flogged and condemned to death but escaped execution. He evangelized among the Morini and Nervii in Flanders and Brabant and became bishop of Rouen around 386/393 (Wace says 'before 390'). In 396 Ambrose of Milan sent him relics of Vitalis and Agricola, for whose arrival he preached De Laude Sanctorum. Summoned to Britain in 394 or 395 to help the bishops there restore peace, probably against Pelagianism, he was later accused of heresy and defended himself at Rome before Pope Innocent I, who sent him the decretal known as the Liber Regularum.
b.s: The library holds his De Laude Sanctorum, a sermon defending the cult of relics against detractors, arguing that contact with the saints' relics heals the faithful and that the saints repay their benefactors by intercession.

b.bio: Vigilius was bishop of Trent from about 380 until his death in 405. The sources say he studied at Athens, where he is said to have known John Chrysostom, and that he was consecrated by Valerian of Aquileia or possibly Ambrose of Milan. As bishop he worked to convert Arians and pagans in the Trentino and beyond it, in the districts of Brescia and Verona. He died on 26 June 405 at Rendena; both the Catholic Encyclopedia and Wikipedia record him as a martyr, and he is patron of Trent and Tyrol.
b.s: The letters held here concern martyrdom: they argue that churches are fittingly raised on martyrdom sites, that confession unto death attains the martyr's crown, and that the faithful dead rest in Abraham's bosom — written against pagan persecutors who compelled converts to sacrifice.

w: Rule for Monks or Eastern Rule

b.bio: Gennadius, De Viris Illustribus no. 51, names Vigilius the Deacon as a resident of Gaul in the second or third decade of the fifth century. Gennadius credits him with a single literary production: a monastic rule based on tradition and read aloud in conventual assemblies. Holsten printed such a rule, substantially derived from Pachomius, in the Codex Regularum (Migne, PL 50). He should not be confused with Pope Vigilius (d. 555), a different man.
b.s: He belongs to the circle of fifth-century Gallic promoters who carried Eastern monastic practice into the Latin West; the works held here are his monastic rule on the abbot's authority, communal property, silence, prayer, and correction.

b.bio: Vincent of Beauvais (c. 1190–1264) — Vincentius Bellovacensis was a French Dominican friar and priest who, apart from visits to Louis IX at Royaumont, spent his religious life at the Dominican house at Beauvais; he served as reader at Royaumont between about 1228 and 1235. His birth date is uncertain (given variously as c. 1184/1194 or c. 1190); he died around 1264. He is remembered chiefly for the Speculum Maius, a vast compilation of universal knowledge begun in the late 1230s and drafted by 1244, which Louis IX read and patronized. He also wrote De eruditione filiorum nobilium on the education of noble children while lector and chaplain to the royal court.
b.s: The library holds only a brief text under his name, Miracles of St. James (PL 163), which treats pilgrimage as requiring prior confession and repentance, presents saints as exercising knightly power for God, and warns of punishment for working on a saint's feast day — hagiographic matter far removed from the encyclopedic Speculum Maius for which he is famous.

b.bio: Viventiolus, also called Juventiole, was a distinguished monk and schoolmaster at Condat (Saint-Oyend-de-Joux / Grand-Saint-Claude) in the Jura before being elected bishop of Lyon (c. 514) on the recommendation of Avitus of Vienne, which see he held until his death. He took part in the Councils of Agaune and Epaon (517) and presided at a Council of Lyon (c. 518) dealing with disciplinary matters. Sources differ on his death date: Wikipedia gives July 12, 524; the New Catholic Encyclopedia says c. 523–524.
b.s: The fragmentary letters preserved in PL 67 concern church discipline: they argue that clerical sins must be publicly corrected rather than silenced, that laypeople may accuse clergy at synod, and that accusers bear the burden of proof — evidence of how conciliar procedure handled accusations against clergy in sixth-century Gaul.

b.bio: Vulgrinus, archbishop of Bourges, received the pallium from Pope Calixtus II in December 1120, his election and consecration being confirmed by letters of the bishops of Clermont, Auxerre and Nevers. He attended the Council of Étampes in 1130 with Hildebert of Tours, where Louis VI recognized Innocent II as pope; but because his province lay under the legation of Girard II of Angoulême, a supporter of Anacletus II, he quietly sided with the antipope. He founded the abbey of Notre-Dame de Loroy and was buried at Saint-Vincent of Le Mans. A different Vulgrin, bishop of Le Mans (1056–1065), appears in the Actus Pontificum Cenomannis and is not this man.
b.s: The letters held here are polemical documents of the Innocent II–Anacletus II schism, arguing for papal legitimacy, episcopal election by suffragans, and excommunication of schismatics and disturbers of the church — chiefly against Girard of Angoulême.

b.bio: The name as the library prints it cannot be securely identified. The only Vitus Winsemius the sources document is a Lutheran who contributed an oration to the memorial volume of speeches delivered at the University of Wittenberg after Philipp Melanchthon's death, published in 1560 alongside Georg Major, Kaspar Peucer, and others. That man belongs to sixteenth-century Lutheranism, not to the Latin Fathers among whom the library shelves this author. No source gives dates, birthplace, or offices for any Winsemius writing patristic material.
b.s: The single item held here is a Preface printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 95; readers should treat the attribution with caution, since the documented bearer of this name was a Lutheran academic orator of 1560, not a patristic writer.
